translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil, archbishop of Caesarea, on not turning toward the affairs of the world, and concerning the fire that then broke out in the city of the Caesareans.
I used to think, beloved, since I am always pricking you in this way with the goad of my word, that my teaching would weary you and seem burdensome to you,
as if I were speaking with excessive boldness words that a man ought not to say when he is himself held by the same errors he speaks about.
But you, on the contrary, have been brought by my reproof to a desire for teaching, and those wounds,
inflicted on you by my tongue, have become for you the cause of greater eagerness. And this is nothing strange,
for you are spiritually wise, as Solomon says in his words: "Reprove a wise man and he will love you."
For this reason then, brothers, I come now too to teach, in the hope that by the power of God I may be able to rescue you from the nets of the devil,
for he brings many and various kinds of battle upon us, beloved, every day.
And he brings upon us, as you know, our own desires, for he has them as arrows against us.
And he always receives from us the power to harm us, for the King bound his great power with a strong bond and did not permit him to destroy the human race entirely.
And from that time on he has no power of his own, but that envious one receives from us the power to harm us through our own folly.
And just as wicked and greedy men, whose occupation it is to grow rich on goods seized from others, and who do not have the power to do this,
then go and sit along the roads, hidden in caves or forests, so as to be unseen by travelers, and thus, when they see travelers coming,
suddenly and unexpectedly fall upon them, so that they cannot escape from them, so too is the wicked devil, our enemy from the beginning:
he hides in the holes of bodily ease, which lie along the road of this life,
in which that robber is able to hide, so that we do not see him, and from there, unseen, he sets snares of destruction for us.
But we, if we wish to pass well along the road of this life and to present soul and body to Christ,
freed from the shame of wounds, and so to receive the crown of victory, must always keep the eyes of the soul moving watchfully about, and
be suspicious toward all the good things of this world, and turn our minds to none of them.
Even if gold lies before you, heaped up in a pile, let your hearts not go out to it, "for if wealth overflows for you,
do not set your hearts on it." Let us not then look upon the good things of the earth, "for our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also await the Savior Christ"),
nor let us rush toward songs and tables and drunkenness, "for vanity of vanities: all is vanity."
Nor let beauty of faces, in which evil spirits dwell, defile us, for the wise man says:
"From the face of a woman, as from the face of a serpent, flee." Nor let powers and rulerships and the glories of men and the height of the throne and splendor deceive us.
and the subjection of cities and nations ("For every man is grass, and all the glory of man is the flower of grass; the grass withers and its flower falls").
For in all these things our enemy lies hidden and waits for the moment when we may turn aside from the straight road and come to his dwellings.
And there is great fear that we may enter into these affairs that seem good, not knowing the hidden evil, and thus swallow, along with the taste of sweetness, the hook of bitter destruction.

And then, some willingly and some unwittingly, we become nailed fast to those affairs, and so they draw us by our thoughts and desires, imperceptibly, toward the terrible dwelling of that robber, which is death.
But for this reason, then, it is good, brothers, that we become like travelers who run swiftly and go lightly,
and thus lighten our souls of the burdens of the world, so as to walk that road without straying and reach a good end.
And let no one suppose that I am a coiner of new names.
For human life has been called a road, since the prophet David too called this life so, when he said:
"Blessed are the blameless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord," and again he cries out to the King:
"Remove from me the way of falsehood," and again, when he sang to God for the help he gives to those in affliction, and played the harp well, he said:
"Who is God, except the God of our God [?], who clothed me with strength and made my walking blameless."
And everywhere he designates human life as a road, whether it is praiseworthy or evil.
For just as those traveling a road always set the steps of their feet ahead of one another in turn, and the foot they have placed in front
they bring behind with the second step, and again they make the front one the rear by the exchange of the other, and thus they reach the end of their road,
so too those who have entered this life by the Creator,
immediately at the very beginning of their life begin to cast the times behind them, and the day that lay ahead they continually turn back behind them, and thus they go on to the end of their life.
Or what do you say? Is not this life such a road and journey, divided by ages as if by miles?
And the beginning of each person's journey is the mother's labor pain and birth, while the end of that course is the grave.
And one person arrives late at the end of his road, and another early;
and one passes through all the stations of the ages, while another does not reach even the first stage of life.
And as for other roads, which go from city to city, it is possible for anyone who wishes not to travel them,
but this road, even if we do not wish to walk it, once it has received us, leads us to the end with no excuse whatever.
And it is not possible, beloved, that one who has once passed through the gate that leads into this life and has entered this road should not reach the end.
But each person, as soon as he comes out of his mother's womb, immediately enters the river and flows along with them, and always that day,
in which he is, he leaves behind his back, and it is no longer possible to return to yesterday, however much he may wish it.
But we rejoice the further forward we press on, as if something were being given to us, when from childhood we become youths and then old men;
and we are too ignorant to understand that all we pass through is lost to us, and we do not perceive the wasting away of our life, and we do not know
when he who sent us out on this road will choose to bring this journey of ours to an end,
or when he will open the door for each of the travellers on this road to come in, and that we must always be ready and wait for the will of the King,
when he makes the end, as he himself says: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps lit, and be like men
who wait for their lord, for when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once."
But we do not wish to understand which are the burdens that are light for this road, which come with us to that lodging,
so that we might gather those that will gladden us there, or which are heavy and troublesome and nailed to the earth,
which are not truly given to men, and which do not fit on that narrow road so as to follow their owners.
Instead, we leave behind those things that we needed to gather, and we gather those that ought to be despised.
For the things that are truly ours and that still come with us, the soul and the body, these we leave thus uncleansed and defiled by the passions, and we pay them no attention,
but those things that are always foreign to us and bring us only shame and nothing else, we never pause from amassing.
We hurry and toil in vain, as if someone were deceiving himself and pouring into a jar pierced with holes.
For I think that everyone, even little children, knows this: that nothing among the good things of this world, over which many are so zealous,
is truly ours, nor will it ever become ours, but it is foreign to everyone, both to those who have acquired it and to those who have none of it.
For if some people gather great and countless gold in this world, would it be theirs forever? God forbid!
Rather, it often flees from them while they are still alive. Though they guard it on every side, it goes away from them in flight.
Or even if they keep it during their lifetime through wretchedness and hardship, yet at the time of death it leaves them and does not wish to go along with its owners.
Instead, they are dragged off by force by the one who separates their souls from that wretched body, and they are led along that unavoidable road.
Then they turn back toward their wealth and weep over their vain labours and the sweat they poured out over it.
But the property passes into another's hands, and leaves to them only the toil they endured for it and the sin of greed.

Nor, if a man should acquire on earth a multitude of possessions by the myriad, and beautiful palaces, and multitudes of flocks and of animals of various kinds, and should clothe himself in all human glory.

does he have any profit from all of it? Rather, for a little while his name is called over it all, and then it is given to others, and he finds only a little earth as his own dwelling place. And often,
before death and the grave and his departure from here, he sees that wealth given to others, and perhaps even his enemies receive it as their inheritance.
Or do we not know how many estates, how many palaces, how many cities and lands pass into the hands of other lords while those who acquired them are still alive?
And how those who were slaves have often been seated on the throne of lordship, while those lords and kings have been counted among slaves through the reversal of affairs?
And as for those contrivances of eating and drinking that evil wealth has devised,
everything beyond what is needed, to fill that ungrateful belly that retains nothing: what of these could become ours?
They leave only a little taste in the palate as they pass through, and they themselves slip away, and then,
as things vexing and oppressive, we expel them from us, for if they linger in the body they bring harm upon us.
For satiety has brought death upon many and has become the cause of their never eating again.
And again, those beds of filth and those defiled unions and all those deeds of a maddened and darkened soul: what are they, what do you say?
Are they not the utter ruin and injury of our nature, the loss of those goods that are truly ours, and harmful to the body as well?
For that evil filth takes away the strength of the body and loosens the firmness of the limbs.
And for this reason each person who has been soiled by those evil beds, at the time
when he has fulfilled that lust of filth, and that frenzy of the flesh subsides and withers, and his mind comes to an understanding of the deed,
like one recovering from heavy drunkenness or awakened from sleep, and he recalls and asks where now is the pleasure of that evil deed,
then he very bitterly repents of that dissolute deed, for he perceives how the body becomes weak and wasted, and negligent and feeble toward necessary tasks.
For this reason people have understood this, and they inscribe the law of chastity in the wrestling places, so that whoever wishes to wrestle
should keep his body from such lusts. And thus they prescribe caution, so that wrestlers should not even look at beautiful faces,
so that in this way they may be crowned, for filth, it says, makes wrestlers blameworthy and not crowned.
So then let us pass by all of this, and let us thus restrain our eyes from looking at these needless things that are not ours, and let us strive to acquire those that are truly ours.
And what is truly ours? First, the soul, by which we live, which is fine,
subtle and rational, and needs nothing of the gross things of this world; and then the body, which was given to it as a chariot by the Creator in this world.
For this is what a human being is: a mind joined to this body, beautifully and skillfully made.
This body is formed in the mother's womb by the all-wise one, the craftsman of all things.

This is the one whom the time of birth brings out into the light from those dark places; this one was set as ruler over all the creatures of the earth; to this one the world has been given for the testing of his virtue;
to this one the law has been given, so that he may become like the Creator as far as his own power allows, and so that he may portray that heavenly order on earth.
This one departs from here, this one stands before the throne of God the Creator, this one is judged, this one receives the recompense for the deeds done here.
But the true possessions are the virtues, when through our struggle they have been woven into our nature,
and they do not abandon us on earth when we are given over to affliction, if only we ourselves do not drive them away by force through the passions.
Rather, when we go there, they run ahead of us and unite those who possess them with the angels, and they shine forever before the eyes of their possessor.
But wealth and glory and luxury, which grow daily through this folly of ours,
these neither entered this life with us, nor do they pass out of it with anyone; rather, what that righteous man once said
has been fulfilled in every person and stands firm: "Naked I came out of my mother's [?] womb, and naked too I am to depart."
And whoever rightly considers what is better for himself, let him devote all his care to his soul,
so that he may save it well and as is fitting, while as for the body, whether it perishes from hunger,
or is punished by cold and heat, or burns with diseases, let him count it as nothing, but in all afflictions let him say the word of the Apostle:
"Though our outer man is wasting away, yet the inner man is renewed day by day."
And let him not be afraid of death or of torments, but let him also say:
"This we know: if this earthly house, our dwelling, is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens."
But if anyone wishes to take care of the body, since it is only the possession of the soul and its helper for living on earth,
let him give it some slight care, only so that it may remain on earth and be alert in the service of the soul, but not so
that it should be stirred up by satiety. But if he ever sees it seeking beyond measure, let him say to it:
"We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out; but let this food and clothing be enough for us,"
for in this way he will lightly climb that ascent to heaven and will make his body a helper of virtue.
But if he allows it to grow haughty and the belly to be filled every day, like some wild beast, in the end he will be overpowered by it and will fall to the ground and lament without profit.
When they bring him before the King and demand from him an account of those times given to him in this world,
and he has nothing to give, then he will mourn long and without profit and will inherit that eternal darkness.
And he will bitterly blame that luxury and his own error, in which he went astray and wasted the time of his life.
And from those tears he will gain nothing, "for in hell who will confess you?" says David.
Let us therefore flee, O brothers, from the affairs of the world with zeal, and let us discipline ourselves well and willingly.
For if anyone has gone astray and has darkened his mind with the care of wealth and bound it with its fetter, or filthiness,
or has brought defilement upon himself, or has stained himself with other sins, let such a person, while there is still time, while complete destruction has not yet come,
lighten the weight of his cargo, and before the ship has entirely sunk, let him throw overboard that abundance of cargo, which is bound to be scattered of itself,
even if he does not scatter it. Let him be like sailors, who, when fierce waves rise against them, even if they have a cargo of great price,
cast it into the sea, and so make the ship ride higher than the waves, so that they may at least be able, with toil, to escape from sinking.
But it is all the more fitting for us to do this, for whatever they throw overboard is immediately lost to them, and the affliction of poverty comes upon them,
whereas we, the more we scatter that evil cargo, the greater the wealth we gather for ourselves.
For when we abandon fornication and things like it, they perish and become nothing, dissolved by tears,
but purity and righteousness abide forever, for these are light things, not to be overwhelmed by the waves.
And again, money that is well distributed is not lost to those who distribute it, but, as if in other ships, strong and large,
it enters the bellies of the poor and is kept safe, and it reaches the harbor of life, and it becomes an adornment for those who distributed it, and not poverty.
Now therefore, beloved, let us too plan something good for ourselves, and this weight of wealth [?].
If we wish that wealth should be ours, let us distribute it to the poor, who will receive it all with joy and will store it in the bosom of the King,
in that fearless treasury, where the moth does not destroy, nor do robbers carry off.
Let us give leave to be scattered to the wealth that we have forcibly held back, so that it may thus go to the poor.
Let us not pass by the Lazaruses lying before our eyes, nor withhold from them the crumbs of our table,
which are enough to fill them; nor let us be like that wicked rich man, so that we may not go to the same Gehenna where he is.
Otherwise we shall then earnestly entreat Abraham and all the righteous, and shall find help from no one, "for a brother cannot redeem; shall a man redeem?"
Rather, each one of them will say to us:
"Do not seek mercy, which you did not show to others, and do not wish to receive such great good things, you who comforted none of those despised ones.
Receive now what you have done in the world. Shed tears, for then you did not have mercy on your weeping brother." All this they will say to us, and justly too.
But I fear lest they speak to us words more bitter than these, for we even surpass that rich man in wickedness,
as you too know, since not only do we spare our wealth and despise the poor and keep our money for our children,
but we also squander that wealth in wickedness and make it a whetstone of sin and a payment for filthiness.
For how many singers and minstrels and actors, men and women, stand at the table of some of us and before the one seated [?] there,
some delighting him with words of filth, and some with their poses and the evil sight of their faces kindling the fire of fornication,
and others, by reviling one another and by joking, stir the one seated there to laughter, and others magnify him with praises and false encomia.
And they then receive a multitude of gifts and money, and they learn from us, through such deeds,
that the practice of filth is better than virtue, since they are honored in this way.
But if a poor man stands before us, who because of hunger is scarcely able to speak, we turn away from that man, who is like ourselves;
we loathe him and hurry to flee from him, as if we were afraid that by walking slowly and being near him his poverty might be passed on to us.
And if he looks at the ground, ashamed because of his affliction, we call him a fraud;
but if he boldly entreats us because of the great distress of his hunger, we call him shameless;
and if he is wearing a whole garment, given to him by someone, we drive him away as greedy and swear that he is feigning poverty;
and if he is clothed in worthless, tattered rags, we chase him away as stinking.
Nor are we ashamed before the name of God, our Creator, which he joins to his entreaties, nor,
when he adjures us by our hope of not falling into those same evils, does he manage to bend our merciless mind.
Because of all this I am afraid of the eternal fire, lest it come upon us more heavily than upon that rich man.
And if time permitted and I had the strength, I would recount all the doings of that rich man and tell you his words.
But now it is time for me to dismiss you, who have grown tired.
But as for you, if I have left anything lacking because of the weakness of my mind and tongue, understand it yourselves and teach your own souls, for:
"Give occasion to a wise man and he will become wiser," says Scripture. "And God is able to multiply all grace among you,
so that always, in all things, you may have help from him and so abound in every good work."
But when our discourse had come to its end, certain brothers turned us back to the path of teaching, for they told us not to pass over
the wonder that the Redeemer performed yesterday, and not to keep silent about how the Savior put the devil to shame, so that we may again give you occasion for hymn-singing.
For, as you know, the devil again displayed his wickedness against us, and armed himself with flames of fire, and came to make war
on the temple of the church; and again the mother of us all prevailed and turned his scheme back upon him, and he gained nothing except this, that he revealed his own malice.
The wind of God's grace arose against those waves of the devil, and calmed them, and kept this temple unharmed.
The devil's winter storm could not shake that rock on which Christ had built the assembly of his flock.
Now he has come to us as well, he who quenched the flame of fire for the youths in Babylon.
Now the devil is deeply grieved, because he could not accomplish his will, that crafty one who kindled that furnace near the church in order to harm this good thing of ours.
And it blazed up on every side, burned the surrounding places and was drawing near to the church, but the Savior turned it back against the one who had kindled it.
And thus the devil drew [?] the bow of his wickedness, but he could not shoot the arrow; and rather he did shoot the arrow,
but that arrow turned back into his own heart, and the mourning he had prepared for us came upon him.
But let us, brothers, make his wound and his mourning more severe. And how? I will tell you, and you do it.
There are some who have had everything they owned burned up by that fire, and they have nothing at all; they saved only their own selves from that evil.
But let us, who have not known the taste of any misfortune, share this wealth of ours with them.
Let us embrace those brothers who barely escaped, and let us say of each one:
"He was dead and has risen, he was lost and has been found," and let us set our consolation against those trials from the enemy,
so that his warfare may become powerless and the harm he has done may come to nothing, and so that he who destroyed the brothers' possessions may be defeated by our goodness.
And you, brothers, who have escaped from that calamity and are deeply grieved over those evils,
do not be so drowned in grief, but drive its fog away from you and strengthen your souls with thoughts of courage.
And make that trial an occasion for winning a crown, so that in this way you may be proved like gold in the furnace, and let us multiply the devil's shame.
When you are not even [?] distressed over those events, remember the fortitude of Job, and you too say, as he did:
"The Lord gave to me and the Lord himself has taken from me; as it pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass."
And let no one entertain an improper thought, so that the Lord's dispensation should seem hard to you, but become like that brave contender and take him as your counselor in what is good.
Consider how many contests he entered, and how many arrows he received from the devil, and yet he was not wounded by even one;
how the devil destroyed all his wealth and sought, by that succession of evil reports, to darken his mind,
for while one was still telling him, another messenger would come, telling of evils worse than those.
And evil followed upon evil, and those trials were like waves, for while one had not yet subsided,
the next would arrive. But that righteous man stood like a rock, unshaken by those waves, and dispersed them like foam, and he spoke that good word:
"The Lord gave to me and the Lord also has taken from me; as it pleased the Lord, so it has come to pass," and he did not consider any one of the things that befell him worthy of a tear.
But when he heard of the death of his children in that house of rejoicing, only then did he tear his garment and show his natural compassion,
and that he was a father who loved his children; yet even then he set a limit to his mourning according to his own measure, adorned the matter with good words and said:
"The Lord gave to me and the Lord himself has taken from me; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done." "May the name of the Lord be blessed,
as if he were saying that I became a father of children for as long as it pleased the Lord." And then again:
"Since he has willed to take away my crown, which he gave me, I will not oppose him. Over those who are his own, let it be as the King wills; he is their creator.
As for me, I am an instrument. Why should I, this servant of his, need useless grief, and why should I blame that command which I have no power to annul?"
With such words the righteous man wounded the devil.
And when the devil saw that he himself was defeated and that he could in no way overcome him, he brought that severe affliction upon Job's very body,
from which worms came forth, and he brought him down from the royal thrones and sat him upon dunghills.
But even in this he stood firm. His flesh was being torn apart, yet the treasure of the fear of God remained unstolen in his soul.
So when the wicked one saw that he could do him no harm at all, he recalled that first deception,
brought about through a woman, and he seized the mind of Job's wife and turned it toward evil, and wished through her to lead the righteous man astray.

And she became fainthearted and stood before the righteous man, bowed down, and she beat her hands together because of the evils, and reproached him with the fruit of his fear of God, and reminded him
of that former prosperity and the distress of that time, and of what kind of things had come upon them in exchange for what kind, and of what profit had come from those many offerings.
So she spoke words befitting the weakness of women, but she could not move his heart at all, as she said:
"I wander about and serve others; I look to my servants and beg from them; and I who used to nourish many am nourished by others.
And it is better to speak evil words, so that in this way we may sharpen the sword of God's wrath, so that he may soon blot us out from the earth, rather than go on living in these evils."
But he was grieved at these words as he had never been grieved at all those great evils, and he filled his eye with anger and turned toward her
as toward an adversary, and said to her: "Why have you spoken thus, like one of the foolish women?
Understand, O woman [?], this counsel of yours. Why do you defile our life with those words, for you have made my life useless too?
Thus I have now reckoned that I have sinned by half, for marriage has made us both one flesh.
But you, behold, have fallen through that blasphemy. If we have received good from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil?
Remember the good things that you had. Weigh that repose against this distress, for no human being's life is blessed in everything.
To be always in good belongs to God alone. But you, if you are aggrieved over these present things, comfort yourself with those that have passed before.
Now you weep, but you have laughed much; now you are poor, but once you were rich. You have drunk the sweet cup of delight; now bear this heavy one too.
For even the water of rivers is not always pure, and our life, you know, is a river, and it flows always and does not cease from flowing.
For some of it has already gone by, some is running its course now, and some has not yet come, and we are all going toward death.
"Now, if we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?"
But we try to force the Judge always to give us good things alone, and we instruct the King how he should order our life.
He has authority over his own commands, and he orders our life as he wishes; he is the fountain of wisdom and knows all that is best.
"But do not scrutinize the commands and judgments of the King. Only let all his work, whatever he does, be pleasing to you.
Whatever he gives you, receive it with joy. Show now, in these afflictions, that you were not unworthy of the joy he gave you before."
Job said such things to her, and he turned aside this scheme of the devil and brought upon him the full shame of defeat.
And then the disease, having come in vain, fled from him. His body returned to health, his life flourished again, and all his wealth came back twofold,
so that he might have the one part as though he had lost nothing, and the second part might be an honor for his righteous endurance.
But why did he receive horses and camels and sheep and all that splendor twofold, while the children given to him were equal in number to those who had died?
Because the beasts and all the other corruptible possessions had perished completely,
those things perished and passed into nonexistence, but the children, even though they had died in the flesh, were alive in the soul.
And since other sons and daughters were given to him by God, he had these twofold as well:
for those who were with him gladdened their parent at that time, while the others had gone on ahead and were waiting for their parent,
so that all of them might then stand around Job, when the Judge of righteousness holds that great assembly, when the trumpet that announces the coming of the King
calls out mightily to those who are in the tombs and brings up the buried bodies from the earth; then the dead will stand in an instant before the Creator.
This, then, as I think, is why it happened that he gave everything else twofold, but the children equal in number to the first ones.
Do you see how many good things Job gained for himself by endurance?
And now you too, if some affliction and trial has touched you yesterday from that devilish fire,
endure it and calm your grief with good thoughts, as Scripture says:
"Cast your thought upon the Lord and he will sustain you," for to him belongs all glory,
honor and worship, to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
